I see the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) is leaving the chamber. He may have found some offence in these remarks. It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that we are the watchdogs of the people's rights. Having heard the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Churchill elaborate in no uncertain terms and with strength of conviction about the objections they have received from organizations, agencies, mining associations and companies as well as from those who are most important, our native people, I think the phrase I used "watchdogs of the people" has meaning. We must have participatory democracy, and this is the only way we can get it. If the government will not listen to those who are directly affected, then I say it is up to the opposition to voice their objections.
The third matter which I believe is of consequence in the role of the opposition is that it must provide constructive criticism to bills which the government introduces. Surely we cannot complain about such a role, because it is important. I think the government, in its charity, will admit that we do have the capacity to understand bills and to submit amendments which will make bills good-not for our sake on this side, not for the sake of hon. members on the other side or for that of the Parliament of Canada but, rather, for the Canadian people.
When I look at Bill C-187, entitled an act respecting minerals in the Yukon territory, I feel that the mining industry is certainly of importance in this country. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra said that we should give due deliberation to this bill as we will to the legislation which will follow the white paper on tax reform. I hope that in the context of the white paper on tax reform and the mining industry, the government will show some understanding of the need for a viable and economic industry. This is what my friends on this side of the House have been talking about. We want do do a thorough job with respect to this matter.
The hon. member for the Yukon and the hon. member for Churchill have indicated that there are at least four main objections to this bill from which we shall not back away because it is necessary that they be implanted in

the government's mind in order that the government has second thoughts on this most important piece of legislation.
But I say to the minister who has just come back to the chamber that what is more important is that the hon. member for Churchill was extremely concerned-I am trying to be as fair as I possibly can-about the lack of understanding by the government regarding the rights of our native peoples. I say this also to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), because for obvious reasons and with my background I feel some comradeship with our native peoples and with the problems with which they are faced.
I am not saying that the government is deliberately ignoring their plight and their pleas, but there seems to be no action. When members on this side point out to the government in no uncertain terms that they are ignoring the aboriginal rights of the native peoples, that they have shown no consistent understanding of their problems, it is time for many more on this side to stand and speak for the rights of our native peoples.

What also concerned the hon. member, and concerns me as a backbencher trying to learn his job, is that every time I am confronted with a bill I find that there are regulatory powers everywhere you look. This is required for flexibility. It is the Big Brother approach. I am told that it is required for efficiency, yet I heard the hon. member say that for the past 50 years these industries have been able to carry on without this type of unwarranted and unnecessary intervention. There is too much regulation. It seems to me that this government is attempting to control the industry to tie it up in knots in order that it can no longer be a viable and economic operation.

The minister shall designate a person to be supervising mining recorder-

subtopic: BAY OF FUNDY-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY ON DEVELOPING TIDAL POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand the question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and I say to him that while at one time, a very long time ago, there was a member-a very good member-of the NDP from the island of Cape Breton, which is part of Nova Scotia, that has not been the case for some time and I do not foresee that it will happen again in the present century. What I am talking about now, so far as the electorate is concerned in the Maritime provinces, is what is happening federally; and federally I believe that in the future, just as at the present time, there will be representatives only from the two major parties in the House of Commons. I may be wrong but I do not think I am.
Members from the Progressive Conservative party and the Liberal party joined together in a manner that I have not known in the years I have been in this House- indeed, 1 am doubtful if it has happened in the past 100 years-to endeavour to see that a re-examination of the programming board's report on the Bay of Fundy tides be carried out by the federal government in co-operation with the governments of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
We in the Progressive Conservative party are in a position to make a good deal of noise because we happen to sit in the opposition, but I would not want it to be thought by the people of the Maritime provinces that the Liberal members of this House are not as dedicated and determined as the members of the Progressive Conservative party to see that this re-examination is carried out. In fact, the decision by the government to carry out the re-examination came only after much pressure had been demonstrated to the public by members of the Progressive Conservative party and by similar pressure being applied by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube) and various other members of the Liberal party in this House, on the minister responsible, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), to see that such an examination was carried out.
In so far as the government's decision to carry out this re-examination was concerned, I am quite certain it was made only because the President of the Privy Council, for instance, placed the problems of the Maritime provinces and the possible solution of those problems ahead of party politics. Certainly that was the case with the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I feel that their particular and unique knowledge of the problem associated with such re-examination assisted materially in the final determination by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to carry out the examination.
I believe that these two cabinet ministers, along with other Liberal members, deserve as much credit as any member of the Progressive Conservative party for seeing that the re-examination is going forward. I think this

April 23, 1971
Request for Bay of Fundy Tidal Power Study stands as an example of what we in the Maritime provinces can do if when we are elected to this Parliament we place the problems of our area ahead of partisan politics and endeavour to accomplish what we all believe will be in the best interests of the people of our area.
I believe that the parliamentary committee, which is non-governmental but is composed of every member from the province of New Brunswick, every member from the province of Prince Edward Island and every member from the province of Nova Scotia, is an indication to the people of the Maritimes that with or without Maritime union we can do much to convince our people and the government, whatever government it might be, that we are determined to solve our own problems, wherever that is possible, by utilizing our own resources wherever they are available. I hope the same approach will be taken to offshore mineral rights as has been taken to Fundy tides. I say that our accomplishments to date, although we are not yet building the dams that will harness the waters that will produce the power, represent a tremendous step forward in the re-examination that is to be carried out.
I can foresee in the very near future the dams being built that will harness the tides that will produce the power that will make the Maritime provinces a "have" area of this nation-not an area that is worried about equalization payments, but an area like Ontario that is more concerned about having to pay additional revenues into the federal treasury to be used in other parts of this nation; because we will no longer be a "have not" area but will be a "have" area and will be able to contribute more than we receive from the federal treasury. It will be quite all right with me when that time comes.
I want to make it positive and clear that so far as Fundy tides are concerned, as Members of Parliament we want every bit of useful information produced to help make a definitive decision. We hope when all the facts are put together they will indicate that the federal government, in co-operation with the private sector of this country, should harness these tides and produce energy. But in order to do this I believe we must consider certain things that the original examination did not take into consideration. One of the matters that unfortunately did not receive the careful attention it warranted concerns what the power produced from the tides would do for the over-all electrical energy system in the Maritime provinces. In other words, Mr. Speaker, those who initially examined the possibilities of harnessing the tides looked too much at what the energy output from Fundy alone would be, rather than examining it from a system point of view within the Maritime provinces.
Fundy tides produce a unique type of power that is best used from a peaking point of view. In other words, they produce a type of power that when placed into the grid is most useful at a time when large volumes of power are required in large sectors of the Maritime provinces or the northeastern United States. This power is not of a value similar to firm power which can be produced in other ways and is saleable at a much cheaper rate than peak power.
It is contended that the input of Fundy power into a grid system provides a type of power, expensive from the point of view of saleability, that would bring great dividends both to our nation and to the industrial community of the northeastern United States. Today we are aware that there is a great desire on the part of the utilities of the northeasern United States to secure additional power. They need it badly because they are facing blackouts and grayouts. Fundy has that power. All we have to do is harness the tides and the market is available.
In determining whether we should harness these tides and supply that market we must discover what the cost will be. We should not be rating the value of this power as compared with firm power; we should be rating it as a unique type of power saleable at a much higher rate. It is in demand to a greater degree than the firm power that can be produced from thermal or hydro energy.
The Americans want to buy our power, but as Canadians naturally we must think of Canada first, and we as Maritimers must first consider what this power can do for our region. At the same time, however, we must accept the fact that initially more power will be generated than we can use. We must also accept the fact that a market is available for it, and indeed we should be negotiating now with the power utilities of the northeastern United States to determine the extent of that market and the value of the power to be produced when the tides are harnessed.
I contend that when we examine what is available from the American point of view in the northeastern United States, coupled with what is now available and will be available in the future in the Maritime provinces, we will find that there is plenty of power to assist both areas at the same time. We will also find that we can look forward to a degree of industrialization in the Maritime provinces that has not yet been imagined. We will also be able to assist in solving a serious problem in the northeastern United States. The great value of this power is that it is pollution free. There is no great danger to the ecology of the Maritime provinces from the harnessing of these tides. There are none of the forbidding drawbacks associated with nuclear energy.
I believe that at the earliest date possible we should get this committee moving and have it examine the papers prepared for the International Conference on the Utilization of Tidal Power. We should do it today rather than the day after tomorrow. I hope that the government is now negotiating with the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to arrange for the re-examination of the programming board's report.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that the personnel who produced the original report should be re-examining it. That would put us in the same position as the private who appealed the decision of a corporal to a sergeant to determine whether it was right, and had it confirmed. The sergeant appealed it to a lieutenant, who confirmed it was right and appealed it to a captain, who confirmed it was right, who appealed it to a major who confirmed it was right. In other words, you get into the position where everybody is confirming what you said was right. I should like new people to examine the programming

April 23, 1971

board's report to see whether they were right and used the proper technology. I am sure that is what the people of the Maritime provinces want.
I believe a number of other things should be involved in this re-examination and I shall list them: First, they should re-study the effect of barriers on tides; second, they should devise a scheme that will supply firm power; third, they should tailor the tidal scheme for the most lucrative power market; fourth, they should restudy projects using simplified lower cost generating units; fifth, they should reassess costs based on the caisson method of construction; sixth, evaluate the export power market and integration of tidal power; seventh, examine maximum use of the new interconnection between New England and the Maritimes for Fundy development; and eight, re-examine competitive power costs in the light of unusual price increases since 1968.
Mr. Speaker, I commend the government for its willingness to re-examine the programming board's report of 1969. I also commend the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources for his attitude throughout the process from the point where it was said there would be no re-examination to the point where today the re-examination is going forward. I commend the President of the Privy Council, the Minister of Veterans Affairs and those members of the Liberal party from the Maritime provinces who have taken a special interest and made a special effort to see that the programming board's report is re-examined. And certainly I congratulate the members of my party who have also shown a determination to have it re-examined.

speechtext: Take your full time.

subtopic: BAY OF FUNDY-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY ON DEVELOPING TIDAL POWER
speechtext:
I should like to take much longer, but my time is limited. I want to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) for placing this motion on the order paper. He has been a long-time advocate of Fundy tidal power and has kept the project alive at times when it seemed nobody was listening. He was also instrumental in forming the all-party House committee actively engaged in studying the subject at this time.
I should like to read an interesting comment which appeared in the Toronto Stock Exchange survey of energy resources in Canada. This confirms some opinions that people recently have made about this project. After referring to the vast power requirements in the next 10 or 15 years both of the United States and of Canada, and mentioning that sources of energy are declining and the United States and Canada are worried about the situation, the article says:
Recent declines in interest rates and the increasing costs of fossil fuels have begun to make the hydro-electric development of the Bay of Fundy tides appear more economically feasible.
Request for Bay of Fundy Tidal Power Study
My main purpose in speaking this afternoon is to put on record, as a member from New Brunswick, that the proposed project is important not only for Nova Scotia but for all Maritime provinces as well as for New England states and the eastern seaboard of the United States. Recently, the Premier of New Brunswick fully endorsed the project. In his remarks he noted that although interest rates are dropping, they still remain high. They are on the downward trend. He noted that environmental pressures have become more urgent and there is a growing realization that tidal power plants, one of our few non-pollution energy producers, must be further developed. He went on to say:
-because of the interprovincial nature of such a project, it would appear that any future undertaking must command heavy federal participation with related lower cost investment capital.
Governor Kenneth Curtis of Maine recently stated that New England is desperately short of power and would probably buy any and all power available from the Fundy project if it is built. He said that he could not think of a project which would be of greater mutual benefit to the New England states and the Maritime provinces.
The chairman of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, Mr. George E. Mclnerney, has gone on record as being strongly in favour of further research and the possible development of Fundy power. New Brunswick faces a growing power shortage, as do most countries today. New Brunswick has a reciprocal arrangement with Maine under which power that is produced in New Brunswick can be sold to Maine. At present Maine is taking all the extra power that New Brunswick can produce.
To take care of the growing power needs of the province, a new $50 million thermal plant is just being completed at Eel River. Nevertheless, the province faces the prospect that all the potential energy from the new plant will be sold and as a result plans are now on the drawing board for a further $50 million thermal plant which is to go into operation in 1975. All this indicates the desperate need of the area for power in the future. The chairman of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission also said that the costs of thermal fuel are steadily going up. The recent increase in oil prices probably prompted him to say that every increase of $1 per barrel in the price of oil represents an additional expense to the province of $4.5 million annually. He therefore feels that serious thought must be given to developing further sources of power such as the Fundy project.
Premier Regan of Nova Scotia has done an excellent job in keeping the project before the public and in keeping it alive. His recent action in forming a corporation to carry on studies relating to the project must be commended. Some people are accusing the Premier of trying to "go it" alone. I do not buy this entirely. I think that his enterprise and initiative must be commended and that he is prepared to co-operate with the other provinces. I emphasize that one province cannot "go it" alone and that if the project is to be successful there must be co-operation between the three provinces, which must

April 23, 1971
Request for Bay of Fundy Tidal Power Study co-operate with the federal government. A recent editorial in the Telegraph Journal reads in part:
The Bay of Fundy is not a Nova Scotia bay. It is at least as much New Brunswick's bay. New Brunswick has a tremendous interest both in what is done with the bay and in the power that it can produce-pollution-free power that would be endlessly renewable and not consume any of the world's shrinking fuel supply. New Brunswick must be involved and must be just as rigorous in pursuit of the idea as Nova Scotia.
The editorial points out that the bay is interprovincial and that therefore the federal government has a definite responsibility to take part in the project and assist the provinces financially because they cannot "go it" alone. The editorial concludes:
The federal government should look at the project with an open pocketbook-
That pocketbook should be just as open for this long neglected region as it was for wealthy central Canada in the 1950s when the St. Lawrence Seaway was built.
That editorial expresses my thoughts aptly. I simply say to all hon. members that the development of Fundy tidal power is worth examining seriously and I make this plea: Let there be a concerted effort to develop the project, an effort which should be made by the three provinces co-operating with the federal government.

Mr. Speaker, I was not surprised to see this notice of motion on the order paper. I welcome this motion. I believe that when an hon. member feels as strongly about a subject as the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates), he is under an obligation to not take no for an answer. I think the forum available to him, the House of Commons, ought to be used on every possible occasion for putting forward his point of view. He ought to do this during the question period, as he has, during budget debates, opposition days and in private members' hour, as he has.
Without doubt, Mr. Speaker, his motion has merit. The matter raised by the hon. member has been the subject of a study. I will not labour that point. Some hon. members may wonder why I am speaking on this matter during private members' hour. I say to the mover of the motion and to the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) that I have lived in northern Ontario for some time and when I have had occasion to go outside Canada I have always been asked, surprisingly, about Niagara Falls and the Bay of Fundy tides? People outside Canada seem to have the idea that these areas are just around the corner from where one lives. I blush in confessing that I have not had the good fortune to see the Bay of Fundy tides. I hope to remedy that situation this summer.

subtopic: BAY OF FUNDY-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY ON DEVELOPING TIDAL POWER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BAY OF FUNDY-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY ON DEVELOPING TIDAL POWER
speechtext:
The Bay of Fundy tides have a magical quality. Their quality permeates not only the area that the hon. member for Moncton represents, not only Nova Scotia and New Brunswick but all of Canada. I strongly suspect that if some way could be found to take the action suggested by the hon. member, Nova Scotia would
certainly benefit as would New Brunswick. Probably the benefits would be even greater, since anything that benefits part of Canada surely benefits the country as a whole.
I have read the report on this subject and undertaken some background studies, and I have read a number of press clippings. As the hon. member for Moncton said, the Premier of Nova Scotia has been criticized in some circles for "going it" alone. Clearly, the point the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North was making was that certain things had to be done and that he was doing them alone. All the same, it was gratifying to hear him pay tribute in this connection to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) and to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube).
I recently read in the Globe and Mail that Mr. R. B. Cameron was appointed president of the recently created Tidal Power Corporation by the Premier of Nova Scotia, Gerald Regan. Then the article reads:
A Crown corporation, the new company was funded at $10 million by legislation at the just completed session of the Nova Scotia legislature to derive power from the Bay of Fundy tides.
The article then says that Premier Regan and Mr. Cameron will leave for Europe to inspect the French tidal power plant in Brittany. It must also be pointed out that the hon. member's motion says, not that the government should consider the advisability of initiating a study but that it should initiate a further study. "Further" is the adjective used. I think this is obligatory because it is incumbent upon those who have the responsibility today to determine whether in this very comprehensive report something was in fact missed, and if there are ways of harnessing this tidal power particularly for the benefit of Canadians in that section of our country.
I want to read a short passage from the Atlantic Tidal Power Programming Board's report. It points to what man has been trying to do and what we are endeavouring to do in Canada. I quote:
Over the centuries, mankind, in his quest for survival and his search for a better way of life, has directed his ingenuity to harnessing the forces of nature to his uses. Mastery and utilization of the energy evident in the sun, the wind, the rivers and the tides as well as of the latent sources existing in various elements of the earth has been a much sought goal, wherein the degree of achievement has grown or varied with the development of technical knowledge and its application and with the economic value of the forces to be harnessed.
In our search for this goal we must face the ever present questions, "Is it financially feasible? Is it in fact economically viable?" I understand from officials of the government that the federal government has offered to join with the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in a general review of the findings of the Atlantic Tidal Power Programming Board and present comments on the proposed development, with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick representatives, regarding a review

April 23, 1971

group comprising a review board and a review committee.
I was interested in the comment by the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) that the same people should not be making the decision. I hope attention will be paid to that representation. The point I am trying to make is that I am in favour of this motion. I salute the hon. member for bringing it forward in another form in this House. It is an opportunity to put forward what I think is a good idea.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too associate myself with the two previous speakers in paying tribute to the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates). He has been a consistent and vigorous advocate of this very important project for a very long time. He was very generous in paying tribute to others. Much could be said about his own unrelenting, thorough, ongoing efforts in which he has fought for this very valuable project. I commend him on his continuing zeal and for the vigour with which he has presented his case, as well as for the thoroughness with which he has mastered the research necessary to make him as much an authority on this matter as a non-technical person can become. Along with the hon. member and other colleagues to whom he has paid tribute, it should be pointed out that some of the newspapers in the Maritime region, desiccated by Davey, were also in the forefront in keeping this very valuable project before the public for consideration.
The Fundy project is not only of concern to the people in areas surrounding the great Bay of Fundy. It is a matter of concern to all in the Atlantic Region because the whole Atlantic region is interested in it. The whole Atlantic region would benefit if this great project should reach actuality. I could go even further. If the region should prosper therefrom, the whole of Canada would benefit because where one region is weak economically the whole country is weakened thereby.
We from the Maritime provinces do not particularly enjoy the "designated area" status. We do not relish pointing out year after year that the pact of confederation, as it is sometimes called, the arrangements of confederation and the tariff and economic adjustments of confederation have placed upon us disadvantages which, added to certain geographical disadvantages, have sometimes been almost intolerable. We do not enjoy constantly harping on these things. We ask that we be given a chance and some assistance in helping ourselves.
I was impressed when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was in Saint John last December. He spoke about the markets to the south, the important markets in New England and the chances for great Maritimes' trade with that area. I think he was profoundly correct. The ties with the economic portion of the great north-east United States has meant a great deal to the Maritimes. The artificiality of our being cut off from economic liaison with that area has been one of the consistent problems facing the Maritimes since their entry into confederation. Anything that can be done to further trade with the
Request for Bay of Fundy Tidal Power Study
northeastern portion of the United States is to be welcomed wholeheartedly. As the mover of the motion has pointed out, the sale of power to a power-deficient area is not only good economics regionally and nationally but internationally as well.
The arguments are compelling for this great project. A former colleague who used to represent Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, now the constituency of South Western Nova in large part, was an expert in engineering and in business. I recall that he gave quite a dissertation on the types of power and the way in which power could be rendered efficient and expanded. He spoke about tidal power as being an inexhaustible source. Very dramatically, Mr. Bower said that as long as the moon, the earth and the sun endure, there will always be tidal power. He said it is an exhaustible source of energy. I was much impressed with that very simple but profound illustration of the situation.
My colleague referred en passant to the question of Maritime union. Maritime union is not a project which greatly excites me. I am still capable of being excited over some things. The regrouping of some provinces, closing down three capitals and building a new provincial legislature would not do much to cope with the real, profound problem, the economy of our region. The development of such things as the Prince Edward Island causeway, the corridor road and the magnificent Fundy power project would be far more important than Maritime union and the studies which might emanate from that project which seem to interest some people.
It strikes me that very often we major in minors on some of the fundamental questions. Here my colleague has directed us to a major. He has done it in a major and important way. I commend him. I hope the study will go forward. I agree with him that not a day should be lost and that indeed too much time already has been lost. I hope that the study will be completed soon and the recommendations will be favourable. This great project will do much for our economy, to strengthen the region and thereby strengthen Canada. We should go forward in this area with the leadership of the provincial governments and the government of the nation which, as my hon. friend from Moncton (Mr. Thomas) pointed out, has responsibilities. Since it has responsibilities and the economic strength, I hope it will accept this obligation.

Mr. Speaker, I was hardly able to rise to my feet in the sense of having been so caught up in the remarks of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), who perhaps more than most of us in this chamber has a gift of using words more effectively on almost any subject, be it a subject of philosophic content or even such a very practical motion as that which is before us today.
I want to associate myself with what has been said by my hon. friend on this side of the House, the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), and each of those very fine speakers who represented what I might

April 23, 1971
Request for Bay of Fundy Tidal Power Study be permitted to call the holy trinity, the three Atlantic provinces so far represented in this debate, and pay tribute to the man in whose name this motion stands, the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates). I suppose, Mr. Speaker, what I was really getting at was this: Does the hon. member feel that the need for federal participation is increased because of the action which has been taken in Nova Scotia? I am referring, of course, to the establishment of the Tidal Power Corporation. Does this make it more urgent that there should be federal participation in the sense of the study being more relevant, or does the situation remain roughly the same?
Be this as it may, we are all aware that the Tidal Power Corporation has been funded to the extent, as I understand it, of $10 million and that a man who it is my pleasure to know, in part at least, from my work on the regional development committee has been appointed president of that Crown corporation, Mr. R. B. Cameron. I for one, was delighted to learn that a man of his ability had been chosen. I think it is widely recognized that Mr. Cameron is a man of unusual gifts. His record in the field of industry and his work in Devco and other places is Well known to all the Maritimes members, especially

those from Nova Scotia. I see both the members from Cape Breton here. They know this situation even better than I do, even though we may not always concur in our assessment of aspects of the situation.
In October, 1969, as is well known-I shall not spend much time on this-the Atlantic Tidal Power Programming Board released its report entitled "Feasibility of Tidal Power Development in the Bay of Fundy." One of the conclusions of that report was that it had become abundantly clear to the board that substantial portions of the large potential tidal power resource of the upper part of the Bay of Fundy were possible of development in a variety of sites and arrangements. In fact, according to the findings of that report, the development of but three of the 23 possible development sites could provide electrical energy in excess of 13,000 million kwh annually.
I hardly need refer to the board's report in much more detail, but the board did conclude-this is some time ago now, and of course the purpose of the motion is to have the issue reopened-that the economic development of tidal power in the bay under conditions prevailing two years ago was not feasible.
I for one must confess this is such an imaginative project that I should be pleased if those who are technically more competent than perhaps any of us in this chamber could see any light at the end of the tunnel, any hope at all that some success may be obtained from further studies in the sense that some program might be developed which could prove economically feasible taking into account some of the additional factors which have been introduced so capably here. I refer to the export of power to the United States, with the large northeastern market available there, taking into consideration the over-all growth, energizing and stimulus effect this would have on the maritime economy and certainly, therefore, in a broad, general way on the economy of all of Canada, even to the perhaps optimistic but certainly intriguing dimensions suggested by the hon. member for Hillsborough. Hon. members will recall he suggested that the day might well dawn, if a feasible project could be constructed and sizeable power realized therefrom, when a province such as Nova Scotia, or since he was speaking for Prince Edward Island, the whole region, I suppose, might become a "have" rather than a "have not" region, to use the colloquial terms with which we are all familiar.
I was impressed earlier today with the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) pointing out the role of the opposition. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that here we see a good example of the role of the private member. A member is able to bring forward a subject for discussion and thereby put it on the record and have some of us respond to a project which certainly is dear to his heart and of value to a whole wide region of our nation.
I hope a study containing some input from the federal coffers might come forward with a proposal for action that would result at least in a portion of the benefits to
April 23, 1971

Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island that have been so glowingly described this afternoon.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, during this hour the House has heard from members representing each of the three Maritime provinces and also from Ontario. As a member from western Canada, I should like to add that we too commend the hon. member for bringing this matter before us. We should like to see the resolution passed.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BAY OF FUNDY-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY ON DEVELOPING TIDAL POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not wish the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to pre-empt exclusively the interest of western Canada in this matter. I do not claim to have any particular familiarity with tidal power. However, energy is a matter of considerable concern in my part of Canada and therefore I should like to speak for a few moments on this interesting resolution.
I suppose the hon. member has already garnered sufficient accolades and congratulations that perhaps he might be able to do without any from me, though perhaps I may say his persistence, as he admitted in his remarks, has in large measure been gratified between the time he placed this resolution on the order paper in the first instance and today, when finally the House has had an opportunity to debate the matter.
A couple of things have occurred in very recent weeks in the over-all field of energy as it affects the Atlantic provinces which have a bearing on the economic feasibility of this particular study. Certainly the price changes in crude petroleum imports to eastern Canada must make alternate energy sources more attractive and be yet another plus factor for this type of project.
Then there is the ongoing exploration for petroleum off the east coast of Canada. We have had some titivating rumours from time to time in this regard, but regrettably nothing of sufficient substance on which to hang anything firm. Nevertheless, in the petroleum industry in Atlantic Canada there is a firm confidence that these exploration efforts will be rewarded with success which, if that is the case, will mean another factor enters the field of supplying energy to Atlantic Canada, a factor that will contribute to its economic well-being.
One hon. member who spoke earlier, I believe the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), pointed out that the federal government has already offered to join with the two provincial governments directly concerned in making a review of the finding of the Atlantic Tidal Power Programming Board. The papers presented at the Halifax meeting of the International Tidal Power Conference in May last year are, of course, available to the federal authorities, and they have been studied very thoroughly. The results of that conference confirm the technical viability of that project; there is no question about that. But regrettably, as the hon. member noted in his motion, the results of that conference did not contribute materially to our knowledge of the economic viability of the project.
Business of the House
The resolution before the House today refers specifically to the interest rates that have applied to federal government projects in the capital works field. Interest rates for major capital projects is a subject that is to be reviewed by this joint study with the two provincial governments. The problem is to determine what the interest rate pattern is likely to be over the next eight to ten years when the project is being built. Federal interest rates for funds advanced to Crown agencies for capital cost programs increased through the 1950s and the 1960s to a peak of about 8i per cent in mid-1970. During the current calendar year this rate has dropped to just below 7 per cent-6-15/16ths per cent-in the present quarter.
This is for all practical purposes the same rate that the Atlantic Tidal Power Programming Board adopted for its studies. The board used the figure of 7 per cent. It should, of course, be noted that commercial rates and borrowing rates by the provinces are likely to be somewhat higher. At the moment I think the prime commercial borrowing rate and provincial borrowing rates are running 8 per cent to 8J per cent per annum. So at the moment it appears there is no indication that interest rates will decline sufficiently to improve the economic viability of the project beyond the information that was available to the programming board.
On the basis of the board's 1969 report, interest rates would have to fall to 3J per cent to 4 per cent in order to make tidal power competitive-when I say competitive, I do not mean cheaper-with other hydroelectric power sources. Therefore, it does not look too promising that interest rates will soon achieve a level that will make the project economically viable.
